newsitem.title: USA: Soybean, cotton prices rise on crop worries.
newsitem.headline: Soybean, cotton prices rise on crop worries.

text.p: Soybean prices rose on Monday as forecasts for frost this week in the Midwest deepened concerns that cold weather had already hurt maturing plants.
Crude oil futures and precious metals eked out slight gains in choppy trade lightened by the Jewish Yom Kippur holiday, which kept a large number of traders out of the oil market, traders said.
November soybeans at the Chicago Board of Trade closed up 3-1/2 cents a bushel at $7.98-3/4.

Meteorologists Monday forecast two cold weather systems would hit the Corn Belt this week, with the first system due late Monday. Only a fraction of corn and soybeans in the main U.S. producing states from Ohio to Nebraska have reached maturity, which prevents freeze damage.
"The frost talk and ideas for a poorer condition rating today, especially on beans, brought beans and meal back," said Steve Bruce of E.D. and F. Man International.

The Agriculture Department in a weekly update on Monday afternoon said 55 percent of the soybean crop was in good to excellent condition, up from 53 percent a week earlier. But it also said soybean growth was several points behind normal. Soybeans were planted late this year.

The department said overall corn conditions improved in the past week, with 62 percent of the crop rated good to excellent compared to 61 percent a week ago. But only 37 percent of the corn crop was mature compared to the five-year average pace of 61 percent.
December corn closed down 1 cent per bushel at $3.13-1/4.

Cotton was buoyed in part by the strength in soybeans, a competing oilseed that is crushed for livestock feed meals and industrial oils. December cotton at the New York Cotton Exchange ended 0.71 cent per pound higher at 76.10 cents.

At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, November lumber futures closed up the $10 daily limit at $350.90 per thousand board feet on indications that supplies from Canada will be tighter appraoching month's end.

Under an agreement with the United States, Canada has a quarterly quota of exports. A trade official of Canada's foreign ministry issued a statement on Monday that export fees might be slapped on Canada's shipments by Sept. 27. Fees are applicable if the quota is hit before Sept. 30.
As of Sept. 23, Canada had shipped 3.712 billion board feet of lumber to the United States since July 1, against a quota of 4.226 billion, according to Canadian government statistics.
On the New York Mercantile Exchange, late buying lifted crude oil for November delivery to close 15 cents higher at $23.37 a barrel, erasing earlier losses.
Heating oil futures, still buoyed by views that inventories could be too low ahead of winter, also finished higher. October heating oil rose 0.06 cent to 67.48 cents a gallon.
Gasoline fell, however, with the October contract dropping 1.02 cents to 60.07 cents.

At the Commodity Exchange in New York, December gold ended up 50 cents at $384.40 an ounce following Friday's slide to a three-year low at $383.30. The December silver contract ended up 3.20 cents at $4.895.

"The complex feels oversold, with everyone bearish and the potential interest rate rise by the Fed at tomorrow's meeting already discounted into current prices, but there could be one more final washout to the downside," North American Equity Services floor trader John Geraghty said.

Analysts said investors had little incentive to buy gold while U.S. inflation remained low, the U.S. Federal Reserve was poised to raise interest rates and the U.S. stock and bond markets remained healthy. Fed policy-makers meet Tuesday to decide whether to raise interest rates.
